claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing materials is governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing materials is governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Nanoscale precipitates pin dislocations.
Nanoscale precipitates reinforce grain boundaries.
Dislocation pinning and grain-boundary reinforcement delay plastic deformation and enhance toughness.
A tailored heat treatment can modify precipitate size, distribution, coherence, and stability.
The relevant structural mediators are nanoscale precipitates within grains and along grain boundaries.
Stable, coherently distributed precipitates mitigate grain-boundary sliding.
Precipitate-mediated dislocation pinning and mitigation of grain-boundary sliding reduce elevated-temperature plastic strain.
Precipitate-mediated dislocation pinning and mitigation of grain-boundary sliding prevent premature toughness degradation at elevated temperatures.
Heat-treated samples with optimized precipitate structures will have a lower creep rate than untreated samples.
Heat-treated samples with optimized precipitate structures will exhibit less plastic deformation than untreated samples.
Heat-treated samples with optimized precipitate structures will have higher fracture toughness than untreated samples.
The hypothesis is restricted to materials whose precipitate-related microstructure can be controlled through thermal treatment.
The hypothesis is restricted to temperatures relevant to fusion plasma-facing operation.
The hypothesis is not expected to govern when severe irradiation effects or other additional factors dominate behavior.
The controlled comparison uses identical alloy samples, with one set receiving the tailored heat treatment and the other remaining untreated.
Both sample sets will be tested under identical high-temperature mechanical conditions.
Creep rate, plastic strain, fracture toughness, and precipitate characteristics will be measured.
Failure of the treated samples to show statistically significant reductions in creep rate and plastic strain together with increased fracture toughness would falsify the proposed mechanism.
